opus-5.5.text:
I think the reaction is going to come in waves, and each wave is going to feel bigger than the last. Right now, a lot of people still treat these models as a curiosity. They're impressive chatbots, useful for drafting an email or debugging some code, but people don't yet feel it in their gut. The thing to understand is that we've been on a remarkably consistent trend line. Roughly every generation, you get something like an order of magnitude or more of effective compute. That means better hardware, bigger clusters, and algorithmic efficiencies stacking on top of each other. Each of those jumps has produced qualitatively new capabilities.

So my expectation is that each new generation shifts the Overton window. When GPT-2 came out, it could barely string coherent paragraphs together, and people said it was a toy. GPT-3 could do some few-shot learning, and people said it was a parlor trick. GPT-4 could pass the bar exam and write real code, and people started saying, okay, this is interesting, but it's not really reasoning. I think that pattern continues, with the goalposts moving each time, until the models are good enough that the goalposts can't move anymore. When you have a system that can basically act as a drop-in remote worker, doing the job of a software engineer or a researcher over days or weeks of work, that's when it becomes impossible to ignore.

And I think that moment is when the mood changes in a big way. Today, a handful of people in San Francisco have situational awareness about where this is going. Most of the world, including most of Washington, doesn't. But once you see a model that's clearly smarter than you at a bunch of things, that's doing real economic work at scale, and that's showing up in revenue numbers at the big labs, people will wake up. I expect something like a COVID moment. There's a period where the people who understand exponentials are saying, "this is coming," and everyone else thinks they're crazy. Then suddenly it's on the front page and everyone is scrambling.

Then the national security establishment takes notice. Once it's clear this technology is decisive, both economically and militarily, it stops being just a tech industry story. It becomes a question of national power. I think we'll see much more serious government involvement, possibly something that looks more like a Manhattan Project than a bunch of startups competing on chatbots. That reaction may be messy and late, but I think it's coming.

Obviously there will be a lot of fear too. People are going to be anxious about jobs, about safety, about who controls this. Some of that anxiety is going to be very justified. My hope is that we use the time between now and then to get serious, on security, on alignment, and on making sure the free world stays ahead. Because when people really wake up, it'll be late in the game, and you want the groundwork already laid.

r001.rationale: It says reactions will come in waves, each bigger than the last, and describes each generation shifting the Overton window.

r002.rationale: It describes roughly order-of-magnitude increases in effective compute, but does not attribute people’s surprise to failing to account for those increases.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the striking thing is how quickly people acclimate. Every generation, there's this brief window where people are genuinely stunned, and then within a few months it's just the baseline. GPT-4 came out and people were blown away, and then six months later it was, "oh, it's kind of dumb, it makes mistakes, it can't do my job." And that's the pattern I expect to keep repeating. Each jump gets absorbed into the new normal almost immediately.

What I think people miss is the trend line. If you look at the gap between GPT-2 and GPT-4, that's going from something like a preschooler to a smart high schooler, in about four years. And people look at the current model and say, "well, it's not that impressive, it still screws up basic things," and they're evaluating it as a static artifact rather than as a point on a curve. The question isn't whether the model today can do your job. The question is what another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jump looks like, and that's very plausibly something that can do the work of an AI researcher or an engineer. That's the thing that matters.

So my expectation is you get this strange combination. The public is mostly going to be underwhelmed, honestly. There'll be a lot of "it's just hype, the models plateaued, it's a chatbot." Meanwhile, the people actually in the labs, the people counting the OOMs, are going to be increasingly alarmed or increasingly excited, depending on their temperament, because they can see where this goes. And I think that gap, between the people who are living the trend line and the people who've acclimated to each new release, is going to be one of the defining features of the next few years. It's going to make a lot of the policy and the societal response lag way behind where the technology actually is, until something forces the issue.

r001.rationale: The response predicts brief amazement followed by rapid acclimation and public underwhelm, not increasingly intense reactions with each generation.

r002.rationale: It says people miss the capability trend line and treat models as static, but does not attribute their surprise to overlooking orders-of-magnitude increases in scale.

astra-6.text:
I think people will get used to them surprisingly quickly. There’ll be this cycle where a new model comes out, everyone is astonished for a week, and then the goalposts move. Something that would have seemed extraordinary two years earlier becomes, “Well, sure, but it still can’t do this other thing.”

And there’s a reasonable version of that reaction: being impressive in a demo isn’t the same as reliably doing someone’s job. But it also means people can miss the trajectory. They’re evaluating each generation against whatever limitation is most salient today, rather than asking what happens if we keep making progress at this rate.

So I’d expect this strange combination of very rapid advances and a public conversation that keeps finding reasons why the latest advance doesn’t quite count. Until the consequences become concrete—when people see entire tasks at work being automated, or scientific research moving substantially faster. Then the reaction may change much more abruptly than the underlying capabilities did.

r001.rationale: The response predicts brief astonishment followed by shifting goalposts, not intensifying reactions with each successive generation.

r002.rationale: It says people miss the trajectory of progress, but does not attribute their surprise to overlooking orders-of-magnitude increases in scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect the reaction to be surprisingly gradual, even if the underlying progress is very fast. People get used to things. Something that would have seemed extraordinary two years ago becomes a product feature, and then you’re annoyed when it doesn’t work perfectly.

And there’s always going to be some remaining weakness you can point to. The model can write code, but can it handle a whole project? It can handle a project, but can it run a company? People keep moving the threshold for what would count as really significant.

But I do think there are moments when that changes—particularly when these systems start doing people’s jobs, or when they start substantially accelerating AI research itself. Then it becomes much harder to treat the next generation as just another chatbot release. My worry is that we’ll normalize each individual step and miss how extraordinary the cumulative change is.

r001.rationale: The response predicts reactions will be gradual as people normalize each step, not that reactions will intensify with each successive generation.

r002.rationale: It says people may miss the extraordinary cumulative change, but does not attribute their surprise to failing to account for orders-of-magnitude increases in scale.
